query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In a single‐phase high-entropy alloy (HEA), brittle behavior emerges not from conventional intermetallic precipitation or solute segregation but from the development of chemical short-range order (SRO) at grain boundaries under service-relevant thermal and mechanical conditions. This local ordering increases the heterogeneity in bonding strength at the boundaries, impeding dislocation nucleation and promoting early crack initiation.
generation.material_initial_state: An as-cast or rapidly solidified single-phase HEA exhibiting homogeneous elemental mixing and a uniform microstructure (with random atomic arrangements and no detectable intermetallic phases or segregation at grain boundaries).
generation.intervention: Subject the HEA to a controlled thermal aging treatment at service-relevant temperatures (e.g., 400–600°C) combined with cyclic mechanical loading designed to stimulate atomic diffusion and localized reordering, but not to induce full phase separation or bulk precipitation.
generation.conditions: Tests performed in an inert or service-representative atmosphere; thermal aging for controlled durations (e.g., tens to hundreds of hours) at 400–600°C with simultaneous cyclic loading (stress amplitude in the elastic to low plastic regime) to mimic engineering service conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of microscopic regions of SRO concentrated at or near grain boundaries, detectable via high-resolution techniques (e.g., atom probe tomography or high-resolution TEM), that locally alter bonding characteristics without forming a separate phase.
generation.mechanism: Thermal activation coupled with cyclic mechanical stress initiates subtle atomic rearrangements in the chemically complex matrix, leading to SRO at grain boundaries. This locally increased order modifies the interatomic bonding landscape—hindering dislocation mobility and promoting crack nucleation—in a manner distinct from classical segregation or precipitate-driven embrittlement observed in conventional alloys.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the as-annealed, homogeneous baseline, the thermally aged and cyclically loaded HEA will exhibit reduced fracture toughness and earlier crack initiation in mechanical tests. Microstructural analysis is expected to reveal increased SRO at grain boundaries rather than signs of conventional grain-boundary segregation or intermetallic formation. In contrast, conventional alloys would degrade primarily due to segregative embrittlement or precipitation.
generation.baseline: The initial single-phase, chemically homogeneous HEA specimen that has not been subjected to the aggressive thermal or cyclic loading conditions, thereby lacking significant SRO development at grain boundaries.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is predicted to be relevant for compositionally complex HEAs under high-temperature, cyclic loading conditions typical of demanding engineering services, provided that the overall phase stability is maintained. It may not apply if the loading/temperature conditions are insufficient to activate notable diffusion or if they exceed thresholds that trigger conventional precipitate formation.
generation.uncertainty: The precise kinetics of SRO development, its spatial distribution at the grain boundaries, and the quantitative relationship between SRO extent and toughness degradation are not fully established. It is also uncertain whether any minor conventional segregative effects might coexist and mask the SRO signature.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA specimens: one retained in the as-annealed, homogeneous state, and another subjected to controlled thermal aging (400–600°C for a set duration) combined with cyclic mechanical loading. Conduct fracture toughness tests (e.g., KIC measurements) on both sets. Characterize the grain boundaries using atom probe tomography and high-resolution TEM to quantify the presence and extent of SRO.
measurements: Fracture toughness (KIC) and crack initiation data
Atomic-scale mapping of grain boundary chemistry via APT
High-resolution TEM imaging of grain-boundary structures
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the thermally aged and cyclically loaded specimens do not show a statistically significant reduction in fracture toughness accompanied by measurable SRO at grain boundaries relative to the baseline, or if toughness degradation is instead primarily associated with conventional segregation or precipitate formation, the hypothesis is rejected.
